author: TK Knewt
text:
It’s good that it comes back down fairly quickly rather then staying high for hours, but spikes into the 11 to 12 mmol/L range, around 200 to 215 mg/dL, still matter even if they are temporary. When glucose rises that high, glycation increases, meaning excess glucose attaches to proteins in your blood and tissues and forms advanced glycation end products. Over time that contributes to damage in blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, and eyes. Higher spikes also increase oxidative stress and inflammation, and they require a strong insulin surge to bring levels back down, which can worsen insulin resistance and strain the pancreas further.
Some people use keeping post meal peaks under 9 to 10 mmol/L, about 160 to 180 mg/dL, as a very early initial target. But that should be a very brief starting point, not the finish line. As insulin sensitivity improves, many people are able to bring their post meal numbers down much further. Ideally, long term, keeping peaks closer to 6.7 mmol/L, or about 120 mg/dL at the top end, is a sign of much better metabolic control. The CGM can help you gradually work toward that tighter range over time instead of just accepting lower than before. Dial in the diet its your best tool. Food is Medicine. Eat a proper human diet of meats, eggs, seafood, healthy fats and above ground veggies. Skip everything else like ultraprocessed foods, refined, carbs, starches and sugars, and dont drink your calories. Best of luck! 🍀
